content: 1. Milestones represent specific, short-term, and tangible steps that need to be taken to achieve the broader, long-term objectives of a program. These milestones, along with targets, should be systematically monitored using a nationally agreed-upon monitoring and evaluation (M&E) framework, which includes clearly defined indicators. 2. A national development plan outlines the overarching development strategy of a government and society. It often includes broad strategies and goals to which the health sector, including immunization programs, can contribute, such as poverty reduction, economic growth, human resource development, and reducing inequalities. The case for investing in immunization becomes stronger when the comprehensive multi-year plan (cMYP) aligns with this national plan or a related strategy. 3. A needs assessment involves gathering information about community knowledge, attitudes, and practices, as well as identifying patterns and causes of illness. This information is then compared to existing services to establish priorities for service development. 4. An objective is a description of a desired achievement that involves a process of change and is aimed at meeting specific needs of identified end users within a defined timeframe. A well-formulated objective is impact-oriented, measurable, time-bound, specific, and practical. Objectives are typically set at a higher level than the expected accomplishments. 5. An outcome refers to a result or accomplishment, such as the percentage of positions filled or the percentage of vaccines funded nationally. 6. An output is the final product or service delivered by a program or project to its end users. Examples include reports, publications, training sessions, advisory services, or logistical support. Outputs are produced to achieve the program’s expected accomplishments and objectives. Outputs can be categorized into broader groups, such as human resource outputs, cold-chain and logistics outputs, or surveillance outputs. 7. Operational planning refers to the planning of recurring activities within systems or programs. It is closely linked to service delivery or management support for service delivery. 8. Priority setting involves determining health priorities based on criteria such as efficiency, equity, impact, feasibility, and alignment with a national health program (NHP). 9. Program management encompasses leading, organizing, mobilizing resources, problem-solving, and directing activities within a system governed by established rules and procedures. In the context of immunization, program management involves applying these functions across the seven components of the immunization system. These rules and procedures include laws, policies, guidelines, and standard operating procedures. 10. A proxy indicator is used when direct indicators to measure a result are difficult to identify. Proxy indicators provide indirect evidence of whether a result has been achieved. 11. Qualitative data refers to information that is not easily expressed in numerical form, although it can sometimes be quantified. It typically consists of words and describes people’s opinions, knowledge, attitudes, or behaviors. 12. Quantitative data refers to information that is measured or measurable in terms of quantity and is expressed in numerical form. It typically consists of numbers. 13. Regulation broadly refers to government intervention in market functions. More specifically, it includes bureaucratic measures such as procedures or rules, supported by laws, economic incentives, or taxes. 14. Reliability refers to the consistency or dependability of data and evaluation judgments. It is determined by the quality of the instruments, procedures, and analyses used to collect and interpret evaluation data. Reliable evaluation information produces similar results when repeated observations are made under similar conditions using similar instruments. 15. A sample is a representative subset of a population selected to assess parameters or characteristics of that population. Random sampling involves selecting a group of subjects (the sample) from a larger population in such a way that each individual or unit has an equal chance of being chosen. 16. Situation analysis is the initial step in planning, which involves identifying the strengths and weaknesses of program performance. It also identifies threats and opportunities for achieving program goals by examining both internal and external factors that influence program outcomes. 17. Stakeholders are agencies, organizations, groups, or individuals who have a direct or indirect role and interest in the objectives, implementation, and evaluation of a program or project. In participatory evaluation, stakeholders take on an active role in the evaluation process as question-makers, evaluation planners, data gatherers, and problem solvers. 18. A strategy in any planning process refers to the description of actions that will outline how planning goals or objectives will be achieved. 19. Supportive supervision is a management style that emphasizes problem-solving, staff support, on-the-job training, feedback, and client involvement. It contrasts with traditional management styles that focus on command, checklists, and correction. 20. Sustainability refers to the ability to maintain a system over time in a way that achieves program goals using resources that are likely to remain available. 21. System and stakeholder networks involve understanding and managing the web of all stakeholders and actors, both individual and institutional, within a system. This includes understanding, including, and managing these networks effectively. 22. Systems thinking is an approach to problem-solving that views problems as part of a broader, dynamic system. Most systems are self-organizing, tightly interconnected, constantly changing, and governed by feedback mechanisms. 23. Strategic planning refers to long-term planning, typically spanning three to five years. 24. A target is a specific objective that defines the number, timing, and location of what is to be achieved. 25. A target group refers to the primary beneficiaries of a program or project who are expected to benefit from its results. They are closely related to the program’s impact and relevance. 26. Triangulation involves using three or more methods to conduct an evaluation or substantiate an assessment. By combining multiple data sources or methods, evaluators aim to reduce bias that may arise from relying on single informants or methods. 27. Validity refers to the extent to which data collection methods or tests accurately measure what they are intended to measure. Valid evaluations consider all relevant factors within the context of the evaluation and appropriately weigh them when formulating conclusions and recommendations.
